Hand-Made Simulations Teaching statistical concepts with jars, tables, and a computer Preface

Hand-Made Simulations Teaching statistical concepts with jars, tables, and a computer Jesus E. Vazquez Draft, November 2026 Preface Students often learn a probability model as a formula first and as an idea second. The book reverses the order. Each chapter starts with a physical activity that students can see and touch, records real data from the activity, and then compares the real data with what a probability model predicts. A computer simulation of the same activity shows what the model would produce if every assumption held. The comparison is the lesson. When the real data and the simulation agree, students see why the model works. When the two disagree, students see which assumption failed and in which direction the estimate moves. The first chapter uses a jar of pebbles to teach the binomial distribution and capture-recapture estimation. The activity was first taught at the University of Maryland in October 2026. All the code runs in base R, and the data from 28 home runs of the activity are included so that readers can reproduce every number. How to read the book. Chapters 1 to 6 follow the order of a class: the idea, the model, the activity, the simulation, the real data, and the application to public health. Chapter 7 collects notes for instructors. The appendix contains the data from the 28 home runs.

Chapter 1 The idea 1.1 Learning goals 1.2 The structure of every chapter

Chapter 1 The idea A hand-made simulation lets students generate data from a process they can watch. The jar activity teaches the binomial distribution through capture-recapture: mark some objects, mix, sample again, and use the share of marked objects in the sample to estimate the total. Students first see the estimator work with pebbles. Next, students see the same formula applied to people, using two clinic lists for Huntington disease (HD). Finally, students see the formula fail when the binomial conditions fail. The physical jar shows a failure the computer does not: cubes and pebbles do not land in the circle with the same probability. 1.1 Learning goals Recognize when a count follows a binomial distribution. Compute binomial probabilities, the cumulative distribution function, and the mean \(np\). Set the expected count \(np\) equal to the observed count \(k\) and solve for the population size \(N\). Predict the direction of the error when an assumption fails. 1.2 The structure of every chapter Each activity in the book follows the same five steps: a physical activity, the model the activity should follow, the real data, the computer version, and the gap between the real data and the computer. The gap is where students learn what an assumption does.

Chapter 2 The binomial distribution 2.1 The formula 2.2 Adding up: the cumulative distribution 2.3 Flipping the question

Chapter 2 The binomial distribution Let \(X\) be the number of successes in \(n\) tries. \(X\) follows a binomial distribution when four conditions hold: The number of tries \(n\) is fixed before the experiment starts. Each try has two outcomes, called success and failure. The chance of success \(p\) is the same on every try. The tries are independent: one try carries no information about the next. Running example. A clinic tests 4 patients for flu. Each patient tests positive with probability 0.25, independently of the other patients. \(X\) is the number of positive tests. 2.1 The formula The probability of exactly \(k\) successes is \[ P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{n - k}, \qquad \binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n - k)!}. \] The term \(\binom{n}{k}\) counts the ways to choose which \(k\) tries are successes; the remaining term is the probability of one such arrangement. The mean is \(E(X) = np\) and the variance is \(\text{Var}(X) = np(1 - p)\). One try has mean \(p\) and variance \(p(1 - p)\), and the binomial adds \(n\) independent tries. For the clinic, \(E(X) = 4 \times 0.25 = 1\) and \(\text{Var}(X) = 0.75\). Exactly one positive test can happen in \(\binom{4}{1} = 4\) ways, so \(P(X = 1) = 4 \times 0.25 \times 0.75^3 \approx 0.42\). 2.2 Adding up: the cumulative distribution The cumulative distribution function adds the probabilities from 0 to \(x\): \(P(X \le 1) = 0.316 + 0.422 = 0.738\). For a count, less than 2 and at most 1 are the same event, and \(P(X \ge 2) = 1 - P(X \le 1) = 0.262\). n <- 4 p <- 0.25 dbinom(0:n, size = n, prob = p) # P(X = k) for k = 0, ..., 4 choose(4, 1) # ways to get exactly one positive pbinom(1, size = n, prob = p) # P(X <= 1) 1 - pbinom(1, size = n, prob = p) # P(X >= 2) c(mean = n * p, variance = n * p * (1 - p)) Check your understanding. The clinic now tests 5 patients, and each tests positive with probability 0.2. The mean is 1, the variance is 0.8, \(P(X = 0) = 0.8^5 \approx 0.33\), and \(P(X \le 1) \approx 0.74\). 2.3 Flipping the question So far, \(n\) and \(p\) were known and the question was about \(X\). Public health often runs the other way: a count is observed, and the question is how large the whole population is. The rest of the chapter asks whether the binomial can count a population that nobody can count directly.

Chapter 3 The jar activity 3.1 Materials 3.2 Protocol 3.3 The jar is a binomial experiment 3.4 The estimator

Chapter 3 The jar activity 3.1 Materials A clear jar with \(N = 126\) objects. Count the objects once in advance and keep the number secret. 21 blue plastic cubes used as tags. A tray or box with a red circle taped on the bottom. The circle is the sample. A whiteboard to record \(M\), \(n\), and \(k\). Figure 3.1: The jar (left) and a drawing of the jar with blue cubes mixed in (right). 3.2 Protocol First toss. Spread the whole jar across the tray. Tag. Swap every pebble inside the circle for a blue cube. The number of swaps is \(M\). Swapping keeps the total \(N\) unchanged. Mix. Pour everything back into the jar and mix well. Second toss. Toss again. Inside the circle, count all objects (\(n\)) and the cubes among them (\(k\)). Estimate \(N\) (Section 3.4). Repeat steps 3 to 5 and record each run. Figure 3.2: First toss, swap, and second toss. 3.3 The jar is a binomial experiment Jar Binomial Cubes swapped in \(M\) Objects in the circle on the second toss \(n\) tries Cubes in the circle successes, \(X\) Share of the jar that is cubes \(p = M/N\) Mixing the jar independent tries Cubes and pebbles equally likely to land in the circle same \(p\) on every try 3.4 The estimator If the jar is well mixed, the share of cubes in the circle should be close to the share of cubes in the jar: \(k/n \approx M/N\). The binomial gives the same answer. The expected number of cubes in the circle is \(E(X) = nM/N\). Setting the expected count equal to the observed count \(k\) and solving for \(N\) gives the Lincoln-Petersen estimator: \[ \hat N = \frac{Mn}{k}. \] Worked example. In run 3 at home, \(M = 21\), \(n = 21\), and \(k = 3\). Cubes are one seventh of the circle, so cubes should be about one seventh of the jar: \(\hat N = 21 \times 21 / 3 = 147\). Of all values of \(N\), 147 is also the value that makes 3 cubes most likely. Figure 3.3: Probability of seeing 3 cubes among 21 objects, as a function of the number of objects in the jar. The Lincoln-Petersen estimator is undefined when \(k = 0\). The Chapman estimator adds one to each count and subtracts one at the end: \[ \hat N_C = \frac{(M + 1)(n + 1)}{k + 1} - 1. \] For run 3, the Chapman estimator gives 120.
simulating.html
Chapter 4 Simulating the jar 4.1 What does a bigger second toss buy?

Chapter 4 Simulating the jar The computer version of the jar follows the binomial exactly: each object in the circle is a cube with probability \(M/N\). All simulations use 1,000 repetitions and set.seed(2026). set.seed(2026) N <- 126 # true total (unknown in practice) M <- 21 # cubes swapped in n <- 21 # objects in the circle on the second toss k1 <- rbinom(1, size = n, prob = M / N) # one toss M * n / k1 # one estimate of N R <- 1000 k <- rbinom(R, size = n, prob = M / N) N_hat <- ifelse(k > 0, M * n / k, NA) summary(N_hat) quantile(N_hat, c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE) # middle 90% of the estimates mean(k == 0) # share of jars with no cubes in the circle Figure 4.1: Estimates from 1,000 simulated jars with N = 126, M = 21, and n = 21. The estimates have a median of 147, and the middle 90% runs from 74 to 441. The distribution is skewed right: tosses with few cubes in the circle divide by a small number and give very large estimates. The distribution also has gaps, because \(\hat N = 441/k\) takes only a few values. About 2% of jars have no cube in the circle. 4.1 What does a bigger second toss buy? sim_jar <- function(n, R = 1000) { k <- rbinom(R, size = n, prob = M / N) ifelse(k > 0, M * n / k, NA) } est_21 <- N_hat est_60 <- sim_jar(60) rbind("n = 21" = quantile(est_21, c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE), "n = 60" = quantile(est_60, c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE)) Figure 4.2: A second toss of 60 objects instead of 21. With \(n = 60\), the median is 126, the middle 90% runs from 84 to 210, and no jar has \(k = 0\). A larger sample narrows the spread of the estimates around the true total.

Chapter 5 My jar at home 5.1 What the real jar showed

Chapter 5 My jar at home I ran the activity 28 times with the real jar (\(N = 126\), \(M = 21\)) and recorded the pebbles and cubes inside the circle on each second toss. The data are in jar-runs.csv. A video of the tosses is at https://youtu.be/LEBHiUieLOI. pebbles <- c(20, 6, 18, 16, 15, 12, 15, 18, 11, 21, 11, 16, 13, 17, 13, 23, 16, 12, 15, 14, 15, 16, 16, 24, 17, 18, 8, 17) cubes <- c(2, 3, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 1, 0, 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 4, 3, 1, 1, 3, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 3) n_home <- pebbles + cubes N_home <- ifelse(cubes > 0, 21 * n_home / cubes, NA) median(N_home, na.rm = TRUE) # 147 21 * sum(n_home) / sum(cubes) # pooled estimate, 155 sum(cubes) / sum(n_home) # 0.14, against 21/126 = 0.17 in the jar median((21 + 1) * (n_home + 1) / (cubes + 1) - 1) # Chapman, 115 5.1 What the real jar showed The estimates ranged from 63 to 336, with a median of 147 and a pooled estimate of 155. One run found no cubes, so the Lincoln-Petersen estimator gave no answer for that run; the Chapman estimator still did, with a median of 115 across all 28 runs. The estimates ran high. On average, 2.4 cubes landed in the circle, while the binomial expects about 3 given the observed values of \(n\). Cubes were 14% of the objects in the circle but 17% of the jar. The cubes were less likely than the pebbles to land in the circle, so \(k\) ran small and \(\hat N\) ran large. The same \(p\) condition failed in the real jar. Figure 5.1: Top: 1,000 simulated jars that follow the binomial. Bottom: 27 home runs with at least one cube. The gap is the lesson. The computer follows the binomial and centers near the truth (median 116). The real jar does not, because a lighter, flatter cube slides differently from a pebble. Ask students why the real estimates might run high before showing the answer.

Chapter 6 From pebbles to people 6.1 Two clinics, two lists 6.2 When the estimate goes wrong 6.3 Who is hard to reach? HD in Mexico

Chapter 6 From pebbles to people HD is a rare inherited brain disorder; a child of a parent with HD has a 50% chance of inheriting the gene. The largest known HD family lives along Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, and blood samples from those families helped locate the HD gene in 1983 and identify the gene in 1993. Across Latin America, many people with HD are never diagnosed or never see a specialist, and many countries have no complete registry. A health ministry needs the count to plan neurologists, genetic counselors, and long-term care. 6.1 Two clinics, two lists Consider two clinics in one region (illustrative numbers). Clinic A has diagnosed 60 people with HD, clinic B has diagnosed 45, and 15 people appear on both lists. The two lists play the roles of the jar: Jar Clinics Cubes swapped in, \(M\) Clinic As list, 60 Objects in the circle, \(n\) Clinic Bs list, 45 Cubes in the circle, \(k\) People on both lists, 15 The same formula gives \(\hat N = 60 \times 45 / 15 = 180\). The Chapman estimator gives about 174. 6.2 When the estimate goes wrong The estimate is only as good as the binomial conditions. The simulation below creates a region with exactly 180 people with HD, 1,000 times, under four scenarios. sim_clinics <- function(scenario, N = 180, R = 1000) { est <- numeric(R) for (r in 1:R) { if (scenario == "Independent lists") { a <- runif(N) < 1/3 b <- runif(N) < 1/4 } else if (scenario == "Referral") { a <- runif(N) < 1/3 b <- ifelse(a, runif(N) < 0.5, runif(N) < 0.167) } else if (scenario == "Hard-to-reach group") { hard <- seq_len(N) <= 60 a <- runif(N) < ifelse(hard, 0.10, 0.43) b <- runif(N) < ifelse(hard, 0.10, 0.33) } else if (scenario == "Separate catchments") { near_b <- seq_len(N) <= N / 2 a <- runif(N) < ifelse(near_b, 0.10, 0.55) b <- runif(N) < ifelse(near_b, 0.50, 0.10) } k <- sum(a & b) est[r] <- if (k > 0) sum(a) * sum(b) / k else NA } est } set.seed(2026) scenarios <- c("Independent lists", "Referral", "Hard-to-reach group", "Separate catchments") res <- lapply(scenarios, sim_clinics); names(res) <- scenarios sapply(res, median, na.rm = TRUE) Scenario Setup Median \(\hat N\) Direction Independent lists \(P(A) = 1/3\), \(P(B) = 1/4\) 181 Centered on the truth Referral \(P(A) = 1/3\); \(P(B \mid A) = 0.5\), \(P(B \mid \text{not } A) = 0.167\) 100 Too small every time Hard-to-reach group 60 people with a 10% chance at each clinic; 120 with 43% (A) and 33% (B) 150 Too small in 86% of runs Separate catchments 90 near B (\(P(A) = 0.10\), \(P(B) = 0.50\)); 90 near A (\(P(A) = 0.55\), \(P(B) = 0.10\)) 340 Too large every time Figure 6.1: Referral, hard-to-reach group, and separate catchments (blue) against independent lists (gray). The dashed line marks the true 180. Referral and a hard-to-reach group make the lists overlap too much, so \(k\) is too large and \(\hat N\) falls short. A hard-to-reach group is the pebble that never lands in the circle. Separate catchments make the lists overlap too little, so \(\hat N\) overshoots. Ask students to predict the direction of each error before showing the histogram. 6.3 Who is hard to reach? HD in Mexico A toy example shows how to read a flow figure. The table lists 200 invented people in five regions. Each row is a region of origin, each column is a region of residence, and the diagonal counts people who still live where they started. Origin / Residence Sur Occidente/Bajo Noreste Centro CDMX Total Sur 25 0 0 5 20 50 Occidente/Bajo 0 20 0 5 15 40 Noreste 0 0 12 3 10 25 Centro 0 2 0 18 15 35 CDMX 0 0 0 5 45 50 Total 25 22 12 36 105 200 The code below draws the table as a flow figure in base R. Each bar is a region: the left bars are sized by origin and the right bars by residence. Each band joins one origin to one residence, and the width of the band is the number of people. par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5)) regions <- c("Sur", "Occidente/Bajo", "Noreste", "Centro", "CDMX") flow <- matrix(c(25, 0, 0, 5, 20, 0, 20, 0, 5, 15, 0, 0, 12, 3, 10, 0, 2, 0, 18, 15, 0, 0, 0, 5, 45), nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(origin = regions, residence = regions)) cols <- c("#4C78A8", "#F2A541", "#54A24B", "#B279A2", "#E45756") gap <- 8 bar_pos <- function(tot) { top <- c(0, head(cumsum(tot + gap), -1)) cbind(top = top, bottom = top + tot) } L <- bar_pos(rowSums(flow)) R <- bar_pos(colSums(flow)) ymax <- max(L[5, "bottom"], R[5, "bottom"]) plot(NA, xlim = c(-0.32, 1.32), ylim = c(ymax, 0), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "") x <- seq(0.04, 0.96, length.out = 60) s <- 3 * ((x - 0.04) / 0.92)^2 - 2 * ((x - 0.04) / 0.92)^3 # smooth S-curve left_used <- L[, "top"] right_used <- R[, "top"] for (i in 1:5) for (j in 1:5) if (flow[i, j] > 0) { l0 <- left_used[i]; left_used[i] <- l0 + flow[i, j] r0 <- right_used[j]; right_used[j] <- r0 + flow[i, j] top <- l0 + (r0 - l0) * s bot <- (l0 + flow[i, j]) + (r0 - l0) * s polygon(c(x, rev(x)), c(top, rev(bot)), col = adjustcolor(cols[i], 0.55), border = NA) } rect(0, L[, "top"], 0.04, L[, "bottom"], col = cols, border = NA) rect(0.96, R[, "top"], 1, R[, "bottom"], col = cols, border = NA) text(-0.01, rowMeans(L), paste0(regions, " (", rowSums(flow), ")"), adj = 1, cex = 0.9) text(1.01, rowMeans(R), paste0(regions, " (", colSums(flow), ")"), adj = 0, cex = 0.9) text(0, -6, "ORIGIN", adj = 1, font = 2) text(1, -6, "RESIDENCE", adj = 0, font = 2) Figure 6.2: Toy example with invented counts: where 200 people were born (left) and where they live now (right). Band width is the number of people. In the toy data, CDMX holds 50 of the 200 people by origin and 105 by residence, while Sur, Occidente/Bajo, and Noreste each lose about half of their people. The real cohort at Mexicos national referral center has the same shape with more regions. Figure 6.3: Where people with HD in a 30-year cohort at Mexicos national referral center come from (left) and where they live now (right). Most of the bands bend toward Mexico City and Estado de Mxico. Moving to Mexico City takes money; low-income families stay in their region, and some never reach any clinic. Those families form the hard-to-reach group, so a two-list estimate comes out too small. An undercount means fewer neurologists and counselors for the people already left out.

Chapter 7 Notes for instructors 7.1 Timing for a 30-minute class 7.2 What happened in the classroom 7.3 Backup plan 7.4 Likely questions 7.5 Ideas for future chapters

Chapter 7 Notes for instructors 7.1 Timing for a 30-minute class Minutes Content 0 to 11 The binomial on the clinic example (Chapter 2) 11 to 20 The jar: activity, binomial mapping, estimator, simulation 20 to 30 HD, two clinic lists, when the estimate goes wrong, summary If the class runs behind, skip the home-versus-computer comparison and say the ethics points in one sentence. 7.2 What happened in the classroom The activity was taught at the University of Maryland on October 28, 2026. The audience responded most to the jar; engagement dipped during the opening binomial basics. Questions at the end asked about the sampling probability across clinics, alternative approaches, and what it means to assume \(N\). Lesson. Open with the jar and teach the binomial on the jar, rather than teaching the formula first and the jar second. 7.3 Backup plan If the live second toss goes badly, for example with no cube in the circle, say so and use the median of the home runs. The point is the method, not one draw. 7.4 Likely questions Why binomial and not hypergeometric? The jar is drawn without replacement, so the hypergeometric is exact. With \(N\) large relative to \(n\), the binomial is close. Is it a problem that the first list was not random? Yes; capture-recapture needs either independent lists or equal capture probabilities. The scenario table gives the direction of the error for each failure. How would you get a confidence interval? The Chapman variance formula, a profile likelihood, or a bootstrap over the two-by-two table. How does the activity connect to missing data? Capture-recapture is a missing-data problem: the cell for people on neither list is missing. 7.5 Ideas for future chapters Each chapter keeps the same five-step structure. Candidates: sampling distributions (drawing from a bag), regression to the mean, confidence-interval coverage, permutation tests (shuffling cards), and missing data (hiding some cards by a rule).
